messages.subject: scheduling infinite capacity and instantaneously
parts:
Hi,

Iñaki was quite right on Twitter, it is possible to schedule a single, persistent change in capacity.  Sorry about that.

It's also possible to schedule infinite capacity, though the results of get_mon_arrivals show a subtle difference when you use `Inf` capacity vs some large number.  Compare schedule1 and schedule2 below.

When scheduling an infinite server to open instantaneously and then immediately shut -- basically a gate that opens from time to time to let the existing queue pass through, then this only works for a large capacity, not an `Inf` capacity.  Compare schedule3 and schedule4 below.  It's a bit of a hack, but I used it to implement the wait-event SimPy example here: https://github.com/nacnudus/simmer-bank/blob/master/18-waitevent.R

``` r
library(simmer)

arrival <- 
  create_trajectory("Arrival trajectory") %>%
  seize("server") %>%
  release("server")

# These two both work, but aren't quite the same.  Both are technically correct,
# though -- my mistake.
schedule1 <- schedule(c(3, 100), c(999, 0))
schedule2 <- schedule(c(3, 100), c(Inf, 0))

# These are designed to implement a gate that opens instantaneously every
# period, and shuts immediately.  Only the first version works.
schedule3 <- schedule(c(3, 3), c(Inf, 0), period = 3)
schedule4 <- schedule(c(3, 3), c(999, 0), period = 3)

## Model/Experiment ------------------------------

set.seed(393939)
env <- 
  simmer() %>%
  add_resource("server", capacity = schedule1) %>%
  add_generator("Arrival", arrival, at(1:9))
env %>% run(until = 12)
#> simmer environment: anonymous | now: 100 | next: 
#> { Resource: server | monitored: 1 | server status: 0(0) | queue status: 0(Inf) }
#> { Generator: Arrival | monitored: 1 | n_generated: 9 }
```

It's also possible to schedule infinite capacity, though the results of get_mon_arrivals show a subtle difference when you use `Inf` capacity vs some large number.  Compare schedule1 and schedule2 below.
